extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary fiction; students of style and creative-writing (fans of Laurence Sterne / Tristram Shandy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit criteria embedded in Tristram Shandy about how to produce the novel's voice and manage the writing/decision process (e.g., alternating moods in composition, tonal aims, selection of material for publication). Useful to writers studying Shandean technique or 18th‑century authorial strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate modes of composition (write 'full' vs 'fasting')
rubrics_metrics.description: My way is this: ... I write one-half full, and t'other fasting;—or write it all full,—and correct it fasting;—or write it fasting,—and correct it full, for they all come to the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method for producing balanced prose: alternate between a 'full' state (free, abundant writing) and a 'fasting' state (restrained, attentive revision) so that one mode counterbalances the other. The passage presents this as a repeatable routine for handling 'nice and ticklish discussions' in writing: produce without inhibition, then impose discretion, or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different compositional moods yield distinct effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When I write full,—I write as if I was never to write fasting again as long as I live... my pen takes its course; and I write on as much from the fulness of my heart, as my stomach. But when ... I indite fasting, ’tis a different history. I pay the world all possible attention and respect,—and have as great a share ... of that under strapping virtue of discretion as the best of you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and harness the predictable differences between compositional moods: 'full' composition produces free, abundant, uninhibited material; 'fasting' composition produces careful, discreet, considered wording. Use the strengths of each mood deliberately to shape tone, candour, and restraint in a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternating moods as a decision-making device ('beds of justice')
rubrics_metrics.description: These my father, humorously enough, called his beds of justice;—for from the two different counsels taken in these two different humours, a middle one was generally found out which touched the point of wisdom...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A procedural rule for resolving difficult choices (literary or practical): deliberate on a question in two distinct states or temperaments (analogized to 'drunk' and 'sober') and seek a compromise or middle course. The author recommends applying this to family, military, and literary decisions—i.e., test ideas under contrasting dispositions to reach balanced outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonal aim: a 'careless, civil, nonsensical, good-humoured Shandean book'
rubrics_metrics.description: So that betwixt both, I write a careless kind of a civil, nonsensical, good-humoured Shandean book, which will do all your hearts good——And all your heads too,—provided you understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the intended aesthetic/resulting voice: combine apparent carelessness with civility and good humour (a controlled nonsense) so the work charms both emotions and intellect. Caveat: such a tone only succeeds if the reader can follow/understand it—so clarity beneath the playful surface is implied as a necessary condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for publication (Yorick's 'moderato' vs 'so, so')
rubrics_metrics.description: There is but one difficulty ... the moderato's are five times better than the so, so's;—show ten times more knowledge of the human heart;—have seventy times more wit and spirit in them;—discovered a thousand times more genius;—and to crown all, are infinitely more entertaining than those tied up with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing material to publish or highlight, prefer pieces that display: deep knowledge of the human heart, wit and spirit, evident genius, and entertaining power. The narrator exemplifies editorial selectivity: print the most engaging and insightful pieces (the 'moderato's') and largely omit the mediocre ('so, so') works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-domain metaphors (musical terms as character markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: What Yorick could mean by the words lentamente,—tenutè,—grave,—and sometimes adagio, as applied to theological compositions... All I know is, that they are musical terms, and have a meaning;—and as he was a musical man, I will make no doubt, but that by some quaint application of such metaphors to the compositions in hand, they impressed very distinct ideas of their several characters upon his fancy,—whatever they may do upon that of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic principle: borrow metaphors and terminology from other arts (here, music) to convey character or tonal distinctions in prose or compositions. Such metaphors can provide vivid, idiosyncratic markers of a piece's character and guide editorial/interpretive judgments.
